Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- In keeping with President Obama's pledge of an administration that is "transparent and accountable," the White House has launched a site that promises to show taxpayers where their stimulus-package dollars are being spent. Visitors to Recovery.gov are greeted with a video message from President Obama. The site, Recovery.gov, allows visitors to track efforts to jump-start a teetering economy in the midst of a slumping housing market and massive job losses. It breaks down the $787 billion package by category: $288 billion for tax relief, $59 billion for health care, and so on. The site promises that more detailed spending information will be posted once federal agencies decide how they are going to allocate the money.  Learn more about where the money is going » . Using graphs, charts and layman's terminology, the online portal is an example of how the tech-savvy Obama administration is taking its message to the American people. While running for president, Obama harnessed the Web's fundraising and social-networking capabilities to energize his grass-roots campaign. And the moment he was sworn in as the 44th president of the United States, administration officials unveiled a sleek interactive version of Whitehouse.gov, the official White House Web site. Recovery.gov, launched within hours of Obama's signing of the stimulus bill Tuesday, continues the theme of offering information in a user-friendly format. Visitors are greeted by a brief video address from Obama. "The American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan represents a strategic and significant investment in our country's future," the president explains. "The size and scale of this plan demand unprecedented efforts to root out waste, inefficiency and unnecessary spending. Recovery.gov will be the online portal for these efforts." The site will publish information on how the stimulus funds will be spent in a "timely, targeted and transparent manner," Obama said. Edward Glaeser, a professor of economics at Harvard University, said transparency has "been a watch word for good government types for years." "There is sense that taxpayers will feel a lot better about this if they actually know where their money is going," Glaeser said. "Better transparency makes evaluation much easier." Glaeser pointed out that the idea behind Recovery.gov is not entirely new. He noted that the Office of Management and Budget has for years had a site where citizens can learn the available cost-benefit information of several government programs. Clicking on "Where is Your Money Going" on the new site brings up a chart displaying key areas where the $787 billion will be distributed, including tax relief, energy, health care and infrastructure and science. Under "Accountability and Transparency," there is a statement that reads, "This is your money. You have a right to know where it's going and how it's being spent. Learn what steps we're taking to ensure you can track our progress every step of the way." Like other Obama online portals, the site encourages user interaction. The public is invited to share stories on how the Recovery Act is affecting them. Scrolling over a map of the United States reveals data on the number of jobs created and saved in each state. Those with some time on their hands can also read, in its entirety, the full text of the legislation.

(CNN) — Reflecting President Obama’s promise to run a government that is “transparent and accountable,” the White House has introduced a new website designed to let taxpayers see how money from the economic stimulus package is being used.

The site, Recovery.gov, opens with a video message from President Obama. It gives the public a way to follow the government’s attempts to revive a fragile economy suffering from a weak housing market and widespread job losses. The website organizes the $787 billion stimulus plan into major sections, including $288 billion for tax cuts, $59 billion for health care, and other categories. It also says that more specific details about spending will be added after federal agencies determine how the funds will be distributed.

Through graphs, charts, and plain-language explanations, the website demonstrates how the technology-focused Obama administration is trying to communicate directly with Americans. During his presidential campaign, Obama used the Internet’s fundraising tools and social networking features to build momentum for his grass-roots effort. Immediately after he took office as the 44th president of the United States, administration officials also released a modern, interactive version of Whitehouse.gov, the official White House website.

Recovery.gov, which went online just hours after Obama signed the stimulus bill on Tuesday, follows the same approach by presenting government information in an accessible format. Users first see a short video statement from the president.

“The American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan represents a strategic and significant investment in our country’s future,” Obama says in the message. He adds that because of the plan’s size and scope, extraordinary efforts are needed to prevent waste, inefficiency, and unnecessary spending. “Recovery.gov will be the online portal for these efforts,” he says.

Obama said the site will provide updates on stimulus spending in a way that is “timely, targeted and transparent.”

Edward Glaeser, an economics professor at Harvard University, said transparency has long been a key principle for advocates of good government. According to Glaeser, taxpayers are more likely to feel comfortable with the program if they can see exactly where their money is going. He also said that greater openness makes it easier to judge how well the program is working.

Glaeser noted, however, that the concept behind Recovery.gov is not completely new. He said the Office of Management and Budget has operated a website for years where people can review available cost-benefit information about various government programs.

On Recovery.gov, selecting “Where is Your Money Going” leads to a chart showing the main areas where the $787 billion will be spent, including tax relief, energy, health care, infrastructure, and science.

In the section labeled “Accountability and Transparency,” the site tells visitors: “This is your money. You have a right to know where it’s going and how it’s being spent. Learn what steps we’re taking to ensure you can track our progress every step of the way.”

As with other Obama administration websites, Recovery.gov is designed to promote public participation. People are encouraged to submit stories describing how the Recovery Act is affecting them. By moving over a map of the United States, visitors can view information about the number of jobs created and preserved in each state. Those who want a deeper look can also read the complete text of the stimulus legislation online.

The site, **Recovery.gov**, was created as part of the administration’s effort to track funds from the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the economic stimulus package intended to boost the struggling U.S. economy through infrastructure projects, tax relief, aid to states and investments in areas such as education, health care and energy.

President Barack Obama has said the public should be able to see where the money is going and whether it is producing results.

The website is expected to include information on federal agency spending, state-by-state funding, grant and contract awards, and eventually details on specific projects supported by stimulus dollars. Officials say the goal is to allow citizens, watchdog groups and journalists to follow the money and report concerns about waste, fraud or abuse.

The administration has promoted the site as a key part of its pledge to make government more open. A recovery oversight board is also tasked with monitoring spending and ensuring agencies comply with reporting requirements.

The stimulus package, passed by Congress amid a deep recession and rising unemployment, represents one of the largest federal efforts in decades to revive the economy. Supporters argue the money is needed to create or save jobs and stabilize state budgets. Critics have questioned the size of the package and warned that rapid spending could lead to inefficient projects or misuse of taxpayer funds.

Recovery.gov is intended to address some of those concerns by making spending data available to the public. However, the site’s effectiveness will depend on how quickly agencies update information and how detailed the reporting becomes as projects get underway.

Administration officials say the website will evolve over time, adding more tools, maps and searchable data as stimulus funds are distributed.

The stimulus package, officially known as the **American Recovery and Reinvestment Act**, was signed into law as the Obama administration works to pull the country out of a deep recession. The plan includes funding for infrastructure projects, education, health care, renewable energy, tax relief, and aid to state and local governments.

Visitors can search for information about stimulus programs, review spending by government agency, and eventually track projects by state and community. The administration says the site will be updated as more data becomes available from federal agencies and recipients of stimulus money.

Recovery.gov also includes tools for oversight, including information about reporting waste, fraud, or abuse. Officials say the goal is not only to inform the public, but also to encourage citizens to help monitor how the money is used.

**White House Uses Recovery.gov to Track Stimulus Spending**

**WASHINGTON** — The White House is pointing Americans to Recovery.gov as a central tool for tracking how billions of dollars from the Recovery Act are being spent, part of an effort to promote transparency around one of the largest economic stimulus programs in U.S. history.

The website, created to monitor spending under the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, allows users to search by state, county, agency and project type to see where federal recovery funds are going. Administration officials say the site is intended to help taxpayers follow the money and hold government accountable.

President Barack Obama has said the goal is to make the spending process more open to the public. “We are going to make sure that every taxpayer dollar is spent wisely and responsibly,” Obama said in remarks about the recovery program. “And we’re going to put information about the spending on a website so that Americans can see where the money is going.”

Recovery.gov includes maps, charts and downloadable data showing grants, contracts and loans tied to the stimulus law. The administration has promoted the site as evidence that it is trying to prevent waste and ensure funds reach communities quickly.

The Recovery Act, passed in 2009 during the depths of the financial crisis, was designed to create or preserve jobs, invest in infrastructure, support state budgets and provide tax relief. Projects listed on the site include road repairs, school improvements, energy upgrades and public safety funding.

Economists say public tracking of stimulus funds can help build confidence, though they caution that transparency alone does not guarantee economic success.

“Recovery.gov is important because it gives the public a way to see how money is being distributed and whether projects are moving forward,” said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “But the real test is whether the spending helps stabilize the economy and supports job growth.”

The White House has argued that the website represents a new standard for federal accountability. Agencies receiving Recovery Act money are required to report spending data, while recipients of funds must provide updates on project status and job impact.

Republican critics, however, have questioned whether the stimulus money is being spent efficiently and whether the reported job numbers accurately reflect the program’s effects. Some watchdog groups have also warned that large federal spending programs remain vulnerable to delays, errors and mismanagement.

Administration officials say they expect Recovery.gov to evolve as more data becomes available, with the goal of giving Americans a clearer picture of how federal dollars are being used in their communities.

For the White House, the site is also a political tool: a way to demonstrate that the administration is acting aggressively to address the recession while inviting the public to monitor the results.

As Obama has put it, the recovery effort is not only about spending money, but about “restoring confidence” that government can respond effectively in a crisis.

**Recovery.gov launches as Obama signs stimulus bill, promising transparency on spending and jobs**

WASHINGTON — Shortly after President Barack Obama signed the $787 billion economic stimulus package into law, the administration launched **Recovery.gov**, a new website designed to show Americans where the money is going, how it is being spent and what results it is producing.

The site is intended to serve as a public dashboard for the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the sweeping legislation aimed at creating or saving jobs, funding infrastructure projects, aiding state budgets and jump-starting an economy deep in recession.

Administration officials described the website as a central tool for accountability, saying taxpayers should be able to track stimulus dollars as they move from Washington to states, cities, contractors and local projects.

“Americans have a right to know where their money is going,” Obama said as he emphasized that transparency would be a core part of the recovery effort.

Recovery.gov includes charts and summaries explaining major categories of spending, including transportation, education, energy, health care and tax relief. The administration says the site will expand over time to include more detailed data on individual projects and contracts.

A key feature is expected to be state-by-state job information. Visitors will be able to see how stimulus funds are being allocated across the country and how many jobs are projected to be created or retained in each state. Officials said the data will be updated as agencies and recipients report spending and employment figures.

The website also invites public interaction. Users can search for information, review spending reports and eventually submit feedback about projects in their communities. The administration has said public scrutiny will help identify waste, delays or misuse of funds.

The launch comes amid intense debate over the stimulus bill. Supporters say the package is necessary to prevent further economic decline and put people back to work. Critics argue that the spending is too large, too fast-moving and vulnerable to political favoritism or mismanagement.

To address those concerns, the law created oversight mechanisms, including reporting requirements and an accountability board to monitor spending. Recovery.gov is expected to work alongside those efforts by making information available not only to government watchdogs but also to ordinary citizens.

Still, the site’s effectiveness will depend on the quality and timeliness of the data it receives. Tracking billions of dollars across federal agencies, state governments and private contractors is a complex task, and some spending details may take months to appear.

For now, Recovery.gov represents one of the administration’s first public tests of its pledge to make government more open. As stimulus money begins flowing, the website is meant to answer a question many Americans are asking: where is the money going, and is it working?

counterfactuals.output:
**Obama Puts Transparency Pledge to the Test With Stimulus-Tracking Website**

President Barack Obama’s promise to bring greater transparency to Washington is facing one of its first major tests with the launch of a federal website designed to let taxpayers track how billions of dollars in economic stimulus money are being spent.

The site, **Recovery.gov**, was created as part of the Obama administration’s effort to monitor spending under the massive economic recovery package passed by Congress in response to the financial crisis and deepening recession. The stimulus law — formally known as the **American Recovery and Reinvestment Act** — directs hundreds of billions of dollars toward infrastructure projects, state aid, tax relief, energy programs, health technology, education and other initiatives intended to create or preserve jobs.

For the White House, the website is more than a public information tool. It is a central piece of Obama’s broader political message: that government can act aggressively in a crisis while still being accountable to citizens.

“We’re going to make sure that every taxpayer dollar is spent wisely and openly,” Obama has repeatedly pledged, framing the stimulus program as both an economic intervention and a new model for federal oversight.

Recovery.gov is intended to give the public a window into where stimulus funds are going, which agencies are distributing them, and what projects are being financed. Administration officials have said the site will eventually include searchable data, interactive maps, agency reports and information about contracts, grants and loans. The goal is to allow ordinary citizens, watchdog groups, journalists and members of Congress to follow the money from Washington to states, cities, contractors and local projects.

The launch reflects a growing belief in political technology circles that transparency is no longer simply a matter of publishing reports after the fact. Instead, public data is increasingly expected to be timely, searchable and usable by people outside government.

During the 2008 campaign, Obama made technology and open government a major part of his platform. His campaign used the internet to organize supporters, raise money and communicate directly with voters, and he entered office promising to apply some of those same digital tools to governing. On his first full day in office, Obama issued a memorandum calling for more transparency, public participation and collaboration across the federal government.

Recovery.gov is one of the earliest and most visible attempts to turn that promise into practice.

The administration has also created the **Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board**, a panel tasked with overseeing stimulus spending and helping prevent fraud, waste and abuse. The board is expected to work with federal agencies to collect data and provide updates through the website. Inspectors general and agency officials will also play a role in monitoring projects and identifying problems.

Supporters say the website could significantly change the relationship between citizens and federal spending. Instead of relying solely on agency press releases or congressional announcements, taxpayers may be able to see how money is allocated in their own communities. A local resident could, in theory, search for road projects, school funding, energy grants or public housing improvements in a particular area and compare promised spending with reported results.

Good-government advocates have welcomed the concept, saying it could create pressure on agencies and contractors to perform responsibly. Public scrutiny, they argue, can serve as a deterrent against mismanagement.

But the project also faces significant challenges.

Tracking federal spending across dozens of agencies and thousands of recipients is technically complex. Money may pass through multiple layers of government before reaching a project, particularly when funds are distributed to states or local governments. Inconsistent reporting standards, delayed updates and incomplete data could limit the usefulness of the site. If the information is too broad or too late, critics warn, Recovery.gov may become more of a public relations portal than a real accountability tool.

There are also political risks for the White House. By promising unprecedented transparency, Obama has raised expectations. If stimulus projects are delayed, if job-creation claims are difficult to verify, or if examples of waste emerge, the same website designed to demonstrate accountability could become a repository of political ammunition for opponents.

Republicans, many of whom criticized the stimulus package as too large and too hastily assembled, are likely to scrutinize the site closely. Some have argued that the administration’s transparency pledge will only matter if the data is detailed enough to reveal questionable spending before money is lost, not merely after it has already gone out the door.

Technology experts also note that publishing data is not the same as making it understandable. For Recovery.gov to succeed, the site will need to present complex budget information in ways that non-specialists can interpret. Maps, downloadable datasets and clear explanations of project status may be essential if the public is expected to use the site effectively.

Still, the launch marks a notable moment in the evolution of digital government. Previous administrations had made federal spending information available online, including through sites such as USAspending.gov, but the stimulus website is tied to a specific, high-profile economic program and backed by a presidential promise of real-time accountability.

The stakes are high. The stimulus package is one of the largest domestic spending efforts in modern U.S. history, and its success or failure could shape public attitudes toward government intervention for years. For Obama, Recovery.gov is meant to show that large-scale spending does not have to happen behind closed doors.

Whether the website fulfills that ambition will depend on the quality of the data, the willingness of agencies to report honestly and promptly, and the ability of citizens and watchdogs to turn raw information into meaningful oversight.

For now, the administration is presenting Recovery.gov as a cornerstone of a new transparency era — one in which taxpayers are invited not just to fund government programs, but to track them.
